summary:
Libya's Penal Code reaches sexual conduct through the offences of "illicit sexual intercourse" and "indecent acts". The indecent-acts provisions carry up to five years' imprisonment. Same-sex relations are not legal for men or women, and where no specific statute reaches the conduct in question, other provisions are applied instead.

Cairo 52's country review finds de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process itself, whether social, medical or surgical, enforced through those same indecent-acts and illicit-intercourse provisions. Recent religious rulings have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible, which narrows the ground on which a trans person can seek care or be seen in public.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. Official identity documents cannot be changed to reflect a person's gender, so a trans visitor or resident presents papers that do not match their presentation.

Hostility toward gender nonconformity is not confined to the statute book. A November 2014 case documented by Human Rights Watch involved a young man targeted by local Islamists in Derna for effeminate dress and "contemporary" clothes, in a period when a militant Islamist group was killing men accused of homosexuality in the territory it controlled.
tangentialFactors:
Extrajudicial violence against people perceived as sexually or gender nonconforming has been recorded in Libya alongside the formal legal penalties. In April 2015 Islamist extremists in Derna executed three young men accused of homosexual acts; reporting at the time noted that information in Derna circulated only through the mosque and concluded that the situation for homosexuals in Libya was deteriorating as militias controlled territory.

In November 2012, twelve men accused of being gay faced torture and threatened death at the hands of a Libyan militia, an instance of post-revolutionary vigilante violence against suspected gay men.

A 2010 French asylum case involved a Libyan girl who was jailed, raped and returned to her family for a forced marriage after stating online that she was gay. The available account gives no age, schooling or student status.

Regional comparison: a 2016 Guardian guide by Brian Whitaker lists Libya among Middle Eastern and North African states where imprisonment is the penalty for homosexuality, with specific terms varying from country to country and other laws used where no specific provision exists.
localsOnly:
Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records no legal protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, services or any other field.

Same-sex relationships are not legally recognised, and LGBTI organisations cannot register, which removes the ordinary route to collective advocacy, service provision and formal complaint.

Religious rulings designating gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible bear directly on residents seeking care over the long term, beyond any individual journey: they constrain what local practitioners and pharmacies will provide.

Family pressure operates alongside state and militia action. The 2010 case of a Libyan girl returned to her family for forced marriage after an online statement indicates that disclosure can be met with confinement and sexual violence within the household as well as by authorities.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Libyan statute that names gender identity or gender expression as an offence. The de-facto criminalisation of transition described by Cairo 52 is attributed to the "indecent acts" and "illicit intercourse" provisions generally; the specific sections, their wording and their application to a trans defendant are not sourced here.

The recent religious rulings designating gender-affirming medical steps impermissible are not attributed to a named authority, a date or a stated scope, so their binding force and geographic reach remain unresolved.

No source in the inventory addresses entry formalities: visa applications, airport screening, customs inspection of hormone medication, or the treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers at Libyan points of entry. Any expectation about border screening would be unsourced.

There is no material on detention conditions for trans detainees, access to hormones or medical care in custody, or sentence implementation. Nor is there sourced information on hate-crime enhancement, on protections for victims of gender-based violence, or on consular notification procedures for foreign nationals.

The Derna and militia violence reporting dates from 2012 to 2015. Territorial control and the operational reach of Islamist groups in Libya at the time of writing are not established by these sources.

The 2010 asylum account lacks the subject's age and any corroboration beyond the encyclopedic entry in which it appears.
